title: How wide is a degree?
hook: Carry one degree of longitude from the equator up to Oslo. How wide is it there?

knows: that latitude and longitude are measured in degrees
doesNotKnow: that a degree of longitude covers less ground away from the equator

misconception: A degree is a fixed distance everywhere.
objective: The learner can explain that meridians meet at the poles, so a degree of longitude shrinks with latitude (half at 60°), while a degree of latitude stays about 111 km.

claims.text: One degree of arc is about 111 km on the Earth (111.2 km on a sphere of radius 6,371 km).
claims.source: pi x 6,371.0088 / 180 = 111.195 km (kit EARTH_RADIUS_KM, IUGG mean radius).

claims.text: On the lesson's globe, a sphere of radius 6,371 km, one degree of longitude at 60°N is 55.6 km, half the equator's 111.2 km; at 80°N it is 19.3 km.
claims.source: Length of a degree along a parallel = 111.195 x cos(latitude): cos 60 = 0.5 gives 55.6 km; cos 80 = 0.1736 gives 19.3 km. v2: 'zero at the pole' removed from the reveal (the slider stops at 80°N); 80°N is quoted at the readout's one decimal (19.3 km), only when the learner stopped there. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. The sphere arithmetic is right (node: pi*6371.0088/180*cos(lat) = 55.598 at 60 N, 19.309 at 80 N, 111.195 at the equator; readouts print 55.6, 19.3, 111.2 and the reveal quotes them). But the sentence states one-decimal values as the length on Earth, and on the WGS84 ellipsoid they are 55.80 km at 60 N, 19.39 km at 80 N and 111.32 km at the equator (pi*a*cos(lat)/(180*sqrt(1-e^2 sin^2 lat))); the lesson's own c4 tells learners the equator degree is 111.3 km, while c2 calls it 111.2. Nothing on the stage or in the reveal says the globe is a sphere (caption: 'A globe.'). Pass 9 verified the old 'about 56' / 'about 19', which hold for the real Earth. Fix (builder): either say the model on stage and in the claim (e.g. caption 'A globe, treated as a sphere of radius 6,371 km' and claim 'On a sphere of radius 6,371 km, ...'), or drop to the precision that holds for Earth ('about 56 km', 'about 19 km', 'about 111 km'). | Builder revision v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, W-243): the stage now names its model. Caption 'A globe, treated as a sphere of radius 6,371 km.' and the reveal's 'Your Seen line, on this sphere of radius 6,371 km: ...' (R_LABEL = Math.round(EARTH_RADIUS_KM)). Readouts unchanged at one decimal. c2 now speaks only of the sphere; c4 speaks of the real Earth (111.3 km on WGS84), so the two no longer give the same quantity two values. Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 27 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node with R = 6371.0088 (kit EARTH_RADIUS_KM) and R = 6371: pi R cos(lat)/180 = 111.195 (equator), 55.598/55.597 (60 N), 19.309 (80 N), which print 111.2, 55.6, 19.3; 2 x 55.6 = 111.2, cos 60 = 0.5. R_LABEL = '6,371'. v3 stage names the model in the caption ('A globe, treated as a sphere of radius 6,371 km.') and the reveal ('Your Seen line, on this sphere of radius 6,371 km: ...'), so the one-decimal values are stated for the sphere; the reveal needs 60 N (seen[60] = '55.6'), and 19.3 is printed only after a stop at 80 N. No motion, no Reset. | Builder revision v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-345): reveal reworded to fit the phone ('On this sphere your Seen line read 55.6 km at 60°N, half the 111.2 km at the equator ... you saw 19.3 km at 80°N'); the current-position clause is cut; readout labels shortened ('1° longitude', '1° latitude', 'Box, 10° wide'); the Equator/60°N/80°N buttons are hidden at the reveal; the Seen line joins with ';'. Sphere still named on the caption and in the reveal ('On this sphere'). Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node with R = 6371.0088 km: pi R / 180 = 111.1951; cos 0 -> '111.2', cos 60° -> '55.6' (exactly half, ratio 0.5000), cos 80° -> '19.3'. Reveal: 'About 56 km' (round 55.6), Seen line '55.6', equator '111.2'; the stage's footnote names the sphere 'radius 6,371 km'.

claims.text: A degree of latitude stays about 111 km everywhere.
claims.source: On the sphere every meridian is a great circle, so 1 degree of latitude = 111.195 km. On the WGS84 ellipsoid it ranges from about 110.57 km at the equator to 111.69 km at the poles (Snyder 1987, USGS PP 1395, ch. 3), so 'about 111 km' holds within 0.6%.

claims.text: On the real Earth a degree of longitude at the equator is 111.3 km, so 'about 111 km' holds.
claims.source: WGS84 semi-major axis 6,378.137 km x pi / 180 = 111.32 km (NGA WGS84 definition). Not shown on the stage; supports the question's 'about 111 km'.

claims.text: Oslo and Helsinki lie at about 60°N.
claims.source: Gazetteer (GeoNames): Oslo 59.91 N 10.75 E; Helsinki 60.17 N 24.94 E. Not opened by the builder (network blocked).

claims.text: Lines of longitude all meet at the poles.
claims.source: Definition of meridians as half great circles from pole to pole. | Builder revision v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-345): reveal reworded to fit the phone ('On this sphere your Seen line read 55.6 km at 60°N, half the 111.2 km at the equator ... you saw 19.3 km at 80°N'); the current-position clause is cut; readout labels shortened ('1° longitude', '1° latitude', 'Box, 10° wide'); the Equator/60°N/80°N buttons are hidden at the reveal; the Seen line joins with ';'. Sphere still named on the caption and in the reveal ('On this sphere'). Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Convention and geometry: meridians are half great circles from pole to pole, so all meet at both poles. The stage draws the box's sides along meridians, and the narrowing as it moves north shows the convergence.

claims.text: The 10-degree box is ten times as wide as one degree of longitude at its middle latitude (for example about 556 km at 60°N).
claims.source: Demo.tsx: box width readout = 10 x pi R cos(lat) / 180 with R = 6,371.0088 km, measured along the box's middle parallel; 10 x 55.6 = 556 km at 60°N. The box's top and bottom parallels are slightly narrower and wider than its middle. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Readout = Math.round(10 x degLonKm(lat)): 556 at 60 N (10 x 55.598), 1,112 at 0, 193 at 80 N (node); labelled 'Box width, 10 deg of longitude', computed on the box's middle parallel. 'About 556 km' also holds on WGS84 (558 km). | Builder revision v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-345): reveal reworded to fit the phone ('On this sphere your Seen line read 55.6 km at 60°N, half the 111.2 km at the equator ... you saw 19.3 km at 80°N'); the current-position clause is cut; readout labels shortened ('1° longitude', '1° latitude', 'Box, 10° wide'); the Equator/60°N/80°N buttons are hidden at the reveal; the Seen line joins with ';'. Sphere still named on the caption and in the reveal ('On this sphere'). Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Readout 'Box, 10° wide' = round(10 * degLonKm(lat)); at 60°N, 10 x 55.598 = 555.98 -> '556 km'. Arc length along one parallel is linear in longitude, so 10° is exactly ten times 1° at the same (middle) latitude, as the claim says.

recall.question: Two towns are 1° of longitude apart. Where are they closest together on the ground?
recall.why: Meridians converge toward the poles, so a degree of longitude shrinks as latitude grows (by the cosine of latitude).
